'Record a goose sighting' accessibility exercise instructions

'Record a goose sighting' is a made-up government service, filled with accessibility issues. Your task is to find them all!

To help find the issues, you will need to use the WAVE accessibility plugin with either Chrome or Firefox. You'll also need to try to complete the exercise using just your keyboard. You should also read these tips on what to look for and how to record your findings.

There are 6 pages in total:

  • Start page
  • Do you like geese?
  • What type of goose did you see?
  • When did you see the goose?
  • Check your answers
  • Confirmation page

Accessibility issues start on the next page. Good luck!

Continue

If you'd like to know more about the background, visit the blog post about this, 'Training people to do accessibility reviews'.

If you'd like to go straight to the answers, view the answers page - no cheating though!

Government Digital Services have recently published how to do a basic accessibility check. If you'd like, you could use these checks as an extension task.

If you're having trouble tabbing, and you're using Firefox or Safari, you might need to enable tabbing.

Accessibility issues in 'Record a goose sighting'

Here is the answer sheet for the 'Record a goose sighting' accessibility testing exercise. There are 19 issues in total (likely 18).

Some of these issues would not be WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) 2.1 failures. But, they could present issues to users with access needs, and WCAG compliance doesn't neccessarily mean that something is accessible.

Many of these problems are missed by automated tools and by a quick keyboard check. See which issues need manual testing and why.

Pages

Start page

Two h1 tags
It is good practice to have only one h1 tag. A h1 tag specifies what the top level heading is for the entire page. It used to be permissible to have another h1 tag nested within a section element, but this was depracated in HTML 5.1. This isn't a WCAG 2.1 failure.
Altered tab order on side menu
The tab order is a bit random, when you're tabbing through the list of links on the right-hand side of the page. This is unpredictable, and a bit disorienting. Whilst it's not a huge issue in this scenario, if the links were further apart on the page, or spread out more, it could cause issues for users who use a screen magnifier or browser zoom. They might not be able to tell where focus is gone, and have to hunt from it, or might have had their screen view dragged across the page as it's following focus (depending on how they've configured their assistive technologies).
Link opens in new tab
Opening a link in a new tab can be appropriate if you tell the user in advance that it's going to happen. This can be done with either with content in the link text or with an icon that has appropriate alternative text. In this case, neither of these techniques have been used. This is an issue because the user may not be aware the the new tab or windows has opened. They then can't use the back button on the keyboard to navigate to where they were, as a new tab history has been opened.
Undescriptive link text
Screen reader users can view links out of context through a links menu. This can be quicker to skim through. If link text doesn't make sense out of context, it would be unusable when viewed this way. The 'More' link on the start page doesn't make any sense out of context - we can infer it means more about geese by seeing that it is in a section titled 'Information about Geese'. This isn't a failure against WCAG 2.1 Level AA criteria but is really useful to do.
Poor focus styling on link
If the focus state style doesn't have a high enough contrast and it can be really hard to tell where focus is. This particularly effects people who have a sight impairement. In this instance, this issue can be fixed by adding the appropriate Design System link class.

Do you like geese page

Missing page title
Some screen readers (like JAWS) read the page title out when a page loads. On this page, there is no title, which means a screen reader user is missing context. An example of a possible page title would be the page question, followed by the service name, and followed by whatever it's hosted on - so 'Do you like geese - Recording a goose sighting - GOV.UK', if it were on GOV.UK.
No legend on the radio button
We can visually tell that the buttons relate to the main heading by looking at the page. But, the question isn't linked up to the element in a way that makes sense for users who can't see. For radio buttons and checkboxes, it's important to have a legend element. The fix would be making sure the 'h1' is inside the 'legend', as per the Design System pattern.
Continue button isn’t keyboard focusable
You can still get past this page by pressing enter when on the radio buttons, but a user might not know this. They might (understandably) expect that the only way to progress is by submitting enter, and so feel trapped and abandon the service at this point. All interactive elements must be usabled with the keyboard. The fix would be removing the tabindex="-1".
Insufficient colour contrast of the form hint
The colour contrast is way too low for the form hint text. In the Design System, it's a darker grey, which does have a sufficient colour contrast ratio. Respecting the out-of-the-box colours and not overriding them here would fix this issue.

What type of goose did you see

Wrong page title
Some screen readers (like JAWS) read the page title out when a page loads. On this page, the page title is 'Boop - Record a goose sighting', which tells the screen reader user nothing about what's on the page. A better format would be the page question, followed by the service name, and followed by whatever it's hosted on - so 'What type of goose did you see - Recording a goose sighting - GOV.UK', if it were on GOV.UK.
Visually hidden item you can tab onto
There is a ghost goose hidden on the page! There is some hidden text on the page, that can be tabbed to. Whilst this isn't a particularly realistic example of this issue, sometimes inputs can get hidden off screen. It can be confusing for keyboard users who are tabbing through the screen, because the focus disappears, and you end up not being entirely sure where or when it's going to reappear, or what would happen if you tried to select the element you were on. If something has focus, it's best that it becomes visible, at least for the duration of it having focus. In many cases think whether there is value for other users by having the content visible at all times.
Placeholder text
Placeholder text disappears when you start to type. This can be confusing, and if you struggle to remember things, you might then need to delete what you've typed in to remind yourself of what was there, in case it was important. It's best to include information like hints outside of the form field, where it can be seen at all times. This is essential if the placeholder text includes important formatting information.

When did you see the goose

No issues on this page!

Sometimes, when you've found issues on other pages, you expect every page to have issues, and you spend a long time looking. However sometimes, some pages don't have issues, and if the basic tests pass, the best use of time is to move on.

Check your answers

Change link - hidden text is incorrect
We talked earlier about links needing to make sense out of context. In this component from the Design System, given the change link is just across from the question, it would look weird to have that visually included in the link. But, we can visually hide text - and that's what is normally done here. A sighted user would see 'change', but a screen reader user would hear 'change what type of goose did you see'. However, it's been configured incorrectly here - and random food items have been put in the visually hidden text, instead of proper text.
Incorrect heading level hierarchy
The heading hierarchy is currently h1 > h3. The 'goose details' heading should be a h2, as it is a direct descendant of the h1. This is an issue because screen reader users can pull all of the headings out into one summary list, as a quick way of skim reading through what is on the page. If the ordering is incorrect like this, it can be hard to interpret when viewed in this way. When heading levels are not included users might also spend time looking for the heading thinking they are missing something.

End page

Use of capital letters
Text that is in all capital letters loses its shape. This can make it harder for some people with dyslexia to read. Unless absolutely necessary (like it is in a reference number), it's best to avoid writing words entirely in capital letters.
Justified text
Justified text forces words and letters to space out a little more than they normally would. This distorts the overall sentence shape a little. This justifying and centering content like this can make it harder to read for some people with dyslexia. The fix would be removing the styling that makes it justify, and allowing it to flow normally. This isn't a failure against WCAG 2.1 Level AA criteria but is really useful to do.
No alternative content for the gif
This gif shows a happy goose celebrating knowledge about geese being shared with the world. This information isn't captured in any other medium like text on the page though, so descriptive alt text needs to be added here. If an img element doesn't have an alt attribute then the href of the image may be read out by screen readers. There is a handy alt decision tree by W3C on how to decide how to write alt text, which is worth a look at.
Animation cannot be stopped.
Moving content such as the happy goose can be a severe distraction for people with conditions such as attention deficit disorders, making it difficult to use the rest of the page. It should run no longer than 5 seconds or be able to be paused or hidden by the users.

Want to learn more about Accessibility?

  • GOV.UK resources about accessibility
  • Udacity course on Accessibility
  • A11y weekly - weekly newsletter about accessibility
  • GDS WCAG 2.1 Primer - a simplified version of WCAG
  • GDS guidance how to conduct a basic accessibility audit

Found any other issues? Want to add more resources? Submit an issue, or create a PR to fix it or add it to this answers list.

Back to the answers

What automation misses

Automated tools catch some of the issues in this exercise. Most of them need a person using the page in a particular way.

This exercise describes 19 issues. Automated checks catch 4 of them. The other 14 need manual checks, judgement, or both.

Detection was assessed with axe-core 4.14 rules and WAVE's published checks. Tools change, and a rule appearing or disappearing is not a statement about WCAG conformance.

Detection by issue

  • Two first-level headings

    steps/start

    Automated
    Not detected
    Manual checks
    visual inspection, heading outline
    Why automation misses it
    The DOM is valid and every heading has text; judging whether two h1s make sense is contextual.

  • Related links appear in a different order to the DOM

    steps/start

    Automated
    Not detected
    Manual checks
    keyboard, visual inspection
    Why automation misses it
    Tools read DOM order; they do not notice that the rendered order differs.

  • External link opens a new tab without warning

    steps/start

    Automated
    Not detected
    Manual checks
    keyboard, content review
    Why automation misses it
    Whether a new tab is expected depends on the link text and the user context.

  • Ambiguous 'More' link text

    steps/start

    Automated
    Not detected
    Manual checks
    screen reader, links list
    Why automation misses it
    Automation can test that a name exists, not whether it is useful.

  • Related links lose their focus indicator

    steps/start

    Automated
    Not detected
    Manual checks
    keyboard, computed styles
    Why automation misses it
    Focus visibility is a rendering outcome; the CSS deliberately removes outline and background.

  • Missing page title

    steps/geese-liked

    Automated
    Detected axe: document-title, WAVE
    Manual checks
    screen reader
    Why automation misses it
    —

  • Radio group has no legend

    steps/geese-liked

    Automated
    Not detected
    Manual checks
    screen reader, forms mode
    Why automation misses it
    The radio buttons are individually named; the missing group name only appears in the interaction.

  • Continue button removed from sequential focus

    steps/geese-liked

    Automated
    Not detected
    Manual checks
    keyboard
    Why automation misses it
    Automated checks test attributes in isolation, not whether every control is keyboard reachable.

  • Low-contrast hint text

    steps/geese-liked

    Automated
    Detected axe: color-contrast, WAVE
    Manual checks
    visual inspection
    Why automation misses it
    —

  • Page title is 'Boop - Record a goose sighting'

    steps/goose-type

    Automated
    Not detected
    Manual checks
    screen reader, content review
    Why automation misses it
    The title is non-empty but meaningless; usefulness is a judgement.

  • Visually hidden, keyboard-focusable 'Ghost goose'

    steps/goose-type

    Automated
    Not detected
    Manual checks
    keyboard
    Why automation misses it
    The element is valid; the problem is where focus goes and what the user can see.

  • Formatting hint only available as placeholder text

    steps/goose-type

    Automated
    Not detected
    Manual checks
    content review, cognitive walkthrough
    Why automation misses it
    Tools cannot know that the placeholder is the only instruction.

  • Change links use incorrect visually hidden text

    steps/check-your-answers

    Automated
    Not detected
    Manual checks
    screen reader, links list
    Why automation misses it
    Accuracy of hidden text is a content judgement, not a structural rule.

  • Heading level jumps from h1 to h3

    steps/check-your-answers

    Automated
    Detected axe: heading-order
    Manual checks
    heading outline
    Why automation misses it
    —

  • All-caps confirmation heading

    steps/end

    Automated
    Not detected
    Manual checks
    visual inspection, dyslexia-aware review
    Why automation misses it
    This is a readability judgement rather than a rule violation.

  • Justified paragraph

    steps/end

    Automated
    Not detected
    Manual checks
    visual inspection, computed styles
    Why automation misses it
    Justification is a typographic outcome that depends on the rendered line lengths.

  • Animated GIF has no alternative text

    steps/end

    Automated
    Detected axe: image-alt, WAVE
    Manual checks
    screen reader
    Why automation misses it
    —

  • Animation cannot be paused or stopped

    steps/end

    Automated
    Not detected
    Manual checks
    visual inspection, motion sensitivity review
    Why automation misses it
    The animation is an image; control availability is not part of its markup.

Using this in a review

A clean automated report is not evidence that a page is usable. For each “Not detected” row, the manual checks column names the technique that exposes the problem. The worksheet is a starting point; the answers describe the defects themselves.

This page is about detection, not conformance. Some of these issues are best practice rather than WCAG 2.1 AA failures, and WCAG compliance does not by itself make a service accessible.
